prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Ice, Crows, Can

outputs.L1: Ice—whole cakes of it. Crows feed on sand. So impoverished is this season that the ground steals color from the shadows of trees. • Can it be that nothing is as far away as here? Just look: how much of the past we have to cover this evening— • Come to think of it, don’t forget to pick off this self and that self along the way. Though that isn’t right—you spit them out like pits. • If there is a partition between the outer and inner worlds, how is it that some water within me churns between the mountain ranges? How is it that we are so easily absorbed by the ground— • Long nights for simple words. • A slant rhyme between current thought and past thought. A late, chewed-over hour, where the long-ago past and the future come to settle scores. • Traveling and traveling, yet so much of the interior remains unpicked over by the eyes. • Nothing is as far away as here.
outputs.L2:
Whole slabs of frozen water. Ravens peck at grit. The season is so barren that even the earth drains the hue from shadows beneath the trees.  

• Could this place be farther away than anything else? Look—what an immense stretch of history we must cross before the night ends.  

• And remember, as you go, to remove one version of yourself, then another. No—that is not quite it. You eject them as though they were fruit stones.  

• If a boundary divides what lies outside from what lies within, why does a body of water inside me surge among mountain chains? Why does the soil take us in with such ease?  

• Plain words require lengthy nights.  

• Present thought forms an imperfect echo of former thought. The hour is late and already thoroughly masticated—the place where the remote past meets the future to resolve old grievances.  

• We keep journeying onward, yet the eyes have left so much of the inner terrain unexplored.  

• Nothing lies at a greater distance than this place.
outputs.L3:
The bleak season is evoked through a series of surreal and desolate images: ice, crows, sand, and shadows drained of color. Together, these elements create a landscape that feels both physically barren and psychologically unsettling. Within this atmosphere, the speaker contemplates the immense distance separating the present from the past. Returning to that past is not a simple act of memory but a difficult journey requiring sustained effort.

As the speaker moves backward through memory, identity emerges as unstable and fragmented. The self is portrayed not as a single, continuous presence but as a collection of different selves accumulated over time. To continue the journey, these former identities must be discarded, abandoned, or carefully separated from one another. This process suggests that revisiting the past also means confronting the many versions of oneself that no longer belong fully to the present.

The poem further complicates the distinction between the inner self and the external world. Images of water, mountains, and absorption into the ground blur the boundary between personal consciousness and the surrounding landscape. The speaker appears at once to travel through the world and to dissolve into it, raising questions about where the self ends and the environment begins.

Ultimately, movement across time and space does not lead to complete self-knowledge. Much of the inner world remains unvisited and unexplored, even after an extensive journey through memory and landscape. This unresolved distance gives force to the central paradox: nothing is as remote or difficult to reach as the place one presently occupies. The present, though seemingly immediate, may be more mysterious and inaccessible than either the past or the farthest physical destination.
outputs.L4:
The poem uses stark natural imagery, fragmented reflection, and recurring paradox to explore the unstable relationship between memory, identity, and time. Its landscapes are not merely physical settings; they also function as projections of the speaker’s inner world. Images of distance, weather, darkness, and open space make the external environment feel both familiar and strange, as though the speaker were moving through a place that belongs simultaneously to the present and the past. Nature therefore becomes a language for experiences that cannot be expressed directly. What lies outside the self reflects what has been hidden, forgotten, or left unresolved within it.

The poem’s fragmented structure reinforces this sense of uncertainty. Rather than presenting memory as a continuous narrative, it offers broken impressions, abrupt shifts, and moments of reflection that resist chronological order. The past does not remain safely behind the speaker; it repeatedly enters the present, altering how the speaker understands both the surrounding world and the self. Time appears layered rather than linear. A current place or sensation can contain earlier experiences, while memory can feel more immediate than the physical present. This movement between temporal perspectives suggests that identity is not fixed but composed of overlapping versions of the self.

Paradox is central to the poem’s meaning. Nearness and distance, presence and absence, movement and stillness are repeatedly brought together. The farther the speaker seems to travel, the more closely the journey returns to what is already within. Likewise, what appears lost or remote remains active in consciousness. These contradictions blur the boundary between inner and outer worlds: landscape becomes memory, memory becomes place, and the act of looking outward becomes a form of self-examination.

The word “here” ultimately gathers these tensions into a single idea. “Here” is not simply a geographical location. It is the point at which past and present, known and unknown, world and self meet. The most distant past is contained within the present because it continues to shape perception, while the unexplored self is also already “here,” waiting to be recognized. The poem thus redefines travel. True travel is not escape into distant places but an inward reckoning with the experiences and identities carried into every place. By confronting the layers of time within the present, the speaker begins to understand that the deepest journey is toward the unfamiliar regions of the self.
outputs.L5:
The lake was sealed beneath a sheet of silver ice. Along the shore, crows gathered around an old tin can, pecking at its frozen edges as if it contained a secret. Their calls echoed through the empty woods while the winter sun hung low in the sky.

A sudden gust sent the can sliding across the ice. The crows followed, hopping and flapping after it, turning the silent landscape into a strange little game. For a moment, even the cold seemed alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about winter, memory, travel, and the porous boundary between the inner and outer worlds. Use fragmented imagery, philosophical questions, and bullet-like separators.
counterfactuals.output:
Winter boards the train without a ticket.

Its coat is lined with abandoned rooms,  
its pockets full of salt, moth wings, foreign coins.

•  

Beyond the glass, fields erase themselves.  
A black tree carries the sky like a nervous system.  
Stations arrive wearing names I almost remember.

Was I ever there—  
or did the place pass through me  
while I slept?

•  

In the dining car, someone stirs snow into tea.  
The spoon circles a small, obedient weather.  
My reflection lifts the cup before I do.

Outside: a village, one red chimney,  
a dog barking at the moon’s locked door.

Inside: the same village,  
but underwater.

•  

Memory does not travel backward.  
It travels sideways, through walls, through wool,  
through the blue seam where the body is stitched  
to distance.

What is a window  
if not the world practicing entrance?

What is a face  
if not weather paused in the glass?

•  

At the border, guards open my suitcase.  
They find a childhood winter folded beneath my shirts:  
the lake with its blind white eye,  
my mother calling from a house of steam,  
a sled moving downhill with no one on it.

They ask: Is this yours?

I say: It remembers me.

•  

The train tunnels into a mountain.  
Darkness becomes intimate—  
a second skull fitted over the first.

For several miles,  
I cannot tell whether I am crossing the earth  
or the earth is crossing me.

Then light: abrupt, surgical.

Snow enters through the eyes.  
Silence enters through the mouth.  
Far away, the horizon opens its empty suitcase.

•  

By morning, I have arrived somewhere  
whose language is made entirely of footprints.

I step down.

The platform breathes beneath my shoes.  
My thoughts scatter into crows.  
The cold puts on my body  
and walks away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental lyric in the style of contemporary avant-garde poetry, beginning with “Ice, entire cakes of it” and ending with “Nothing is as far as here.”
counterfactuals.output:
Ice, entire cakes of it  
stacked in the blue pantry of noon—  
each one humming  
a small electric winter.

We carried spoons.  
We carried maps of spoons.  
The mouth was a country  
crossed out by weather.

Meanwhile, the elevator  
learned the word *elsewhere*  
and opened onto wheat,  
onto static, onto a room  
where our shadows sat before us  
wearing our names backward.

Who left the faucet dreaming?  
Who folded the hospital light  
into a paper animal  
and released it down the hall?

I touch the wall:  
it becomes distance.  
I touch distance:  
it rings, unanswered.

Inside every object  
another object evacuates—  
chair from chair,  
salt from salt,  
the bright machinery from snow.

We arrive by disappearing.  
We speak in doors.  
The sky lowers its unfinished face.

Nothing is as far as here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
The road unspools beneath a moon that has forgotten our names; each mile closes like an eye behind us.

•

In the abandoned station, all the clocks contain the same hour—your hand departing from mine, again and again.

•

I find an old self folded inside a suitcase, still wearing the dust of a country that never existed.

•

Beyond the salt flats, black trees lift their empty branches, signaling to stars already dead.

•

We walk there without bodies, our shadows dragging their long thirst across the white earth.

•

At dusk, you enter the room behind my ribs, where the furniture is covered and something keeps breathing beneath the sheets.

•

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn the themes of a harsh season, crows, mountain ranges, memory, and psychological self-examination into a dense prose poem with repetition and occasional rhetorical questions.
counterfactuals.output: Winter came without ceremony, a hard white verdict laid across the fields, and the crows were the only handwriting left legible. Black wing, black branch, black cry—again and again they crossed the pale air as if carrying pieces of a burned message toward the mountains. The mountains remembered nothing, or remembered too much. Their blue ranges rose behind one another like thoughts I could not finish, like old injuries weather had polished into distance. I stood beneath them and searched myself: What have I kept alive by refusing to name it? What have I buried that still circles overhead? The crows answered with hunger. The wind answered with my own voice made strange. Harsh season, harsh season: every pond locked its dark eye, every road narrowed into silence, every tree held up its empty hands. Yet memory moved under the ice, slow and sleepless, pressing its face to the cold glass. I remembered the room, the door, the words I did not say; I remembered them differently; I remembered remembering, which is the crueler country. Beyond me, the ranges repeated themselves—ridge after ridge, refusal after refusal—and within me another range lifted, jagged with shame, bright with old snow. How far must a person climb into himself before he becomes weather? How many black birds must rise before grief admits it has wings? The crows gathered, scattered, gathered. I counted them until counting became confession. I watched them vanish into the bruised pass, each one taking nothing from me, each one taking everything, while winter tightened its iron around the world and the world, severe and shining, said: Look again. Look again. Look again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a meditative, surreal poem in which a traveler reflects on how the past and future converge, how identity is shed along the way, and how distant places can feel strangely immediate.
counterfactuals.output:
At the station where no trains arrive,  
I sit beneath a clock of rain.  
Its hands move both ways, gathering  
the hour I left  
and the hour that waits for me  
into one clear drop.

The road has taken my names.  
One fell among the pines,  
one sleeps in a border guard’s ledger,  
one became the word for salt  
in a language I could not keep.

Now I travel lightly—  
a coat, a cup,  
a shadow with no allegiance.

Behind me, my childhood opens  
like a door ahead.  
Beyond it, the old years  
are still preparing my arrival:  
my mother lifts a lamp,  
my unborn hands reach for its flame.

How near the far countries are.

A desert enters the room  
as a little red dust on my shoe.  
The moon over another ocean  
rests in the spoon beside me.  
Somewhere, bells are ringing  
in a city I have never seen,  
and their bronze circles  
pass through my ribs.

Perhaps distance is only  
the body’s way of dreaming.

Perhaps time is a traveler  
who sheds face after face  
at every inn,  
until the mirror holds  
no one—

and no one, looking back,  
contains the road, the vanished names,  
the station, the rain-clock,  
the future kneeling in the past,

and every distant shore  
breathing here,  
inside this single  
unclaimed breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
